module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-! # Erdős Problem 349

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos349

open Set Filter Real Nat Function


/--
This defines the core property of the problem: For what values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$
is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete?
-/
def IsGoodPair (t α : ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsAddComplete (range (fun n ↦ ⌊t * α ^ n⌋))

/--
For what values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete
(that is, all sufficiently large integers are the sum of distinct integers of the form $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$)?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_349 :
    {(t, α) | 0 < t ∧ 0 < α ∧ IsGoodPair t α} = answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
It seems likely that the sequence is complete for all
for all $t>0$ and all $1 < \alpha < \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t)
    (hα : α ∈ Set.Ioo 1 ((1 + √5) / 2)) : IsGoodPair t α := by
  sorry

/--
For any $k$ there exists some $t_k\in (0,1)$ such that the set of $\alpha > 0$
such that the sequence $\lfloor t_k\alpha^n\rfloor$ is complete consists of at least $k$
disjoint line segments, that is, it has at least $k$ connected components.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem exists_t_for_k_disjoint_segments (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ t ∈ Ioo 0 1,
      let S := {α | 0 < α ∧ IsGoodPair t α}
      k ≤ (connectedComponentIn S '' S).encard := by
  sorry

/--
Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are odd infinitely
often and even infinitely often?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halves_odd :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {n | Odd ⌊(3/2 : ℝ) ^ n⌋}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are even infinitely often?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halves_even :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {n | Even ⌊(3/2 : ℝ) ^ n⌋}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- For $\alpha > 2$ and any $t > 0$, the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is not additively
complete; equivalently $(t, \alpha)$ is not a "good pair". A partial result on the open Erdős
Problem 349: it complements `complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio`.

The proof is recorded via the `formal_proof` mechanism rather than written inline, as it exceeds
the repository's proof-length guideline. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
  "https://github.com/cepadugato/formal-conjectures/blob/23c629bc2347864782ce88f957a64d6567b978a1/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/349.lean#L87"]
theorem alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t) (hα : 2 < α) : ¬ IsGoodPair t α := by
  sorry

/-- For $0 < \alpha \le 1$ and any $t > 0$, $(t, \alpha)$ is not a good pair: every term
$\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ lies in the finite interval $[0, \lfloor t\rfloor]$ (since
$\alpha^n \le 1$), so every subset sum is bounded by the constant $\sum_{i \in [0,\lfloor t\rfloor]} i$,
and no large integer can be a subset sum. A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349,
complementing the $2 < \alpha$ and integer-coefficient cases. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
  "https://github.com/cepadugato/formal-conjectures/blob/erdos-349-integer-characterization-proof/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/349.lean"]
theorem alpha_le_one_not_isGoodPair (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t) (hα0 : 0 < α) (hα1 : α ≤ 1) :
    ¬ IsGoodPair t α := by
  sorry

/-- **Binary expansion.** Every natural number $k$ is a sum of distinct powers of two: there is
a finite set $E$ of exponents with $k = \sum_{i \in E} 2^i$. Proved by strong induction:
subtract the largest power $2^m \le k$, recurse on the remainder. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
  "https://github.com/cepadugato/formal-conjectures/blob/erdos-349-integer-characterization-proof/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/349.lean"]
theorem exists_finsetSum_two_pow (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ E : Finset ℕ, k = ∑ i ∈ E, 2 ^ i := by
  sorry

/-- **The pair $(1, 2)$ is good.** The powers of two $\lfloor 1\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 2^n$ form an
additively complete set: every $k \ge 1$ is a finite sum of distinct powers of two. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
  "https://github.com/cepadugato/formal-conjectures/blob/erdos-349-integer-characterization-proof/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/349.lean"]
theorem one_two_isGoodPair : IsGoodPair 1 2 := by
  sorry

/-- **The dyadic fiber at $\alpha = 2$.** For every $k$, the pair $(1/2^k, 2)$ is good: the
sequence $\lfloor 2^n / 2^k\rfloor$ is additively complete because at index $n = m + k$ it equals
the exact power $2^m$, so its range contains all powers of two, which already form an additively
complete set. Uses monotonicity `IsAddComplete.mono`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
  "https://github.com/cepadugato/formal-conjectures/blob/erdos-349-integer-characterization-proof/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/349.lean"]
theorem dyadic_two_isGoodPair (k : ℕ) : IsGoodPair (1 / 2 ^ k) 2 := by
  sorry

/-- **Integer leading coefficient $t \ge 2$ blocks completeness.** For every integer base
$\alpha$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ with integer $t \ge 2$ is not good: $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor =
t\alpha^n$ is a multiple of $t$, so every subset sum is too, but two consecutive large integers
cannot both be multiples of $t$. Generalizes the parity obstruction ($t = 2$). A partial result
on Erdős Problem 349. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
  "https://github.com/cepadugato/formal-conjectures/blob/erdos-349-integer-characterization-proof/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/349.lean"]
theorem int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair (t : ℤ) (ht : 2 ≤ t) (α : ℤ) :
    ¬ IsGoodPair (t : ℝ) (α : ℝ) := by
  sorry

/-- **Erdős Problem 349, complete characterization on positive integer pairs.** For integers
$t \ge 1$, $\alpha \ge 1$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ is good (i.e. $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is
additively complete) iff $(t, \alpha) = (1, 2)$. Assembles the four partial results: $(1,2)$ is
good, $\alpha \le 1$ fails, $2 < \alpha$ fails (`alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair`), and integer
$t \ge 2$ fails. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
  "https://github.com/cepadugato/formal-conjectures/blob/erdos-349-integer-characterization-proof/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/349.lean"]
theorem integer_isGoodPair_iff (t α : ℤ) (ht : 1 ≤ t) (hα : 1 ≤ α) :
    IsGoodPair (t : ℝ) (α : ℝ) ↔ t = 1 ∧ α = 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos349

findings.description:
`IsGoodPair t α := IsAddComplete (Set.range fun n : ℕ ↦ ⌊t * α ^ n⌋)` takes subset sums of the SET of values, so a value that occurs at several indices can be used only once. The source's completeness is a property of the SEQUENCE, with terms counted by index. ⌊tαⁿ⌋ repeats values whenever tαⁿ(α−1) < 1, so the two notions differ, and not only in degenerate cases.

Machine-checked witness (standard axioms; /workspace/review/cex2.lean and cex3.lean): t = 180/289, α = 17/10, so S_t(α) = (1,1,3,5,8,15,25,43,73,…).
(i) `IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n : ℕ ↦ ⌊(180/289:ℝ) * (17/10)^(n+1)⌋)` holds. This is the source's notion; the proof uses Brown's criterion, and it is an instance of Graham's Theorem 2.
(ii) `¬ IsGoodPair (180/289) (17/10)` holds. The range {0,1,3,5,8,15,…} satisfies a_k + a_{k+1} ≤ a_{k+2} (because α² > α+1), and 2 is not a subset sum while 1 < 2 < 3. By Folkman's argument (Graham 1964, Thm 1), 2, 10, 35, 108, … are never subset sums.

This is not isolated. A grid computation over (0,1)×(φ,2) finds about 11% of it (area ≈ 0.04) complete in the source's sense but not `IsGoodPair`: Graham's area of ≈ 0.85 of complete points drops to ≈ 0.81. Exact spot checks at (3/10, 37/20) and (7/10, 33/20) agree.

Degenerate case as well: S(t,1) = (1,1,1,…) is complete for 1 ≤ t < 2, but `IsGoodPair t 1` is false (machine-checked for t = 1).

Secondary issue: the sequence starts at n = 0, whereas ErGr80 and Graham define S(t,α) = (s₁, s₂, …). For t < 1 the extra term ⌊t⌋ = 0 is harmless, and in general it only reparametrises t ↦ tα. But it is why the file counts (1,2) as good, although S(1,2) = (2,4,8,…) is not complete.
findings.source_evidence: ErGr80 (Erdős–Graham, Old and new problems…, 1980), §6, pp. 53–54: "For a sequence A = (a₁, a₂, ...) ... let P(A) = {Σ εₖaₖ : εₖ = 0 or 1, Σ εₖ < ∞}" ... "the sums are restricted by the multiplicity any particular term can have" ... "Let us call a sequence S = (s₁, s₂,...) of integers complete if P(S) contains all sufficiently large integers." p. 57: "Let S(t,α) = (s₁, s₂, ...) with sₙ = [tαⁿ]. For what values of t and α is S(t,α) complete?" (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf). Graham, Acta Arith. 10 (1964) 63–70, the paper cited for the remark: S_t(α) = (s₁, s₂, ...), sₙ = [tαⁿ]; complete means n = Σ εₖsₖ with εₖ ∈ {0,1}. Theorem 2: "If 0<t<1 and 1<α<5^{1/3} then S_t(α) is entirely complete"; its proof lists the possible starts "(1, 2, m, ...)" and "(1, 1, m, ...) for m ≤ 3" (https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/64_02_erdos.pdf). erdosproblems.com/349 cites [ErGr80, p.57].

findings.description:
The requested answer set {(t,α) | 0<t ∧ 0<α ∧ IsGoodPair t α} is not the set the source asks for. IsGoodPair measures completeness of the set of values of ⌊tαⁿ⌋, not of the sequence (see the IsGoodPair finding).

Concretely, (180/289, 17/10) is in the source's answer set: S_t(α) = (1,1,3,5,8,…) is complete (Graham 1964, Thm 2; machine-checked via IsAddCompleteNatSeq'). It is not in the Lean set (¬ IsGoodPair (180/289) (17/10), machine-checked).

The discrepancy covers:
- an open region of the unit square (0,1)×(1,2), of area ≈ 0.04 (numerical estimate), which is exactly the region whose answer Graham's paper determines explicitly;
- the line α = 1, 1 ≤ t < 2 (source: complete; Lean: not good).
The n = 0 indexing also shifts the set by (t,α) ↦ (tα,α). So a correct description of the source's answer does not answer the Lean problem, and vice versa.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/349: "For what values of t,α ∈ (0,∞) is the sequence ⌊tαⁿ⌋ complete ...? [ErGr80, p.57]". ErGr80 p. 57: "Let S(t,α) = (s₁, s₂, ...) with sₙ = [tαⁿ]. For what values of t and α is S(t,α) complete?", with completeness defined via P(S) = {Σ εₖsₖ} (§6). Graham 1964, Theorems 2–6, determines this set inside 0<t<1, 1<α<2 (area ≈ 0.85), using index-based sums.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the faithful definition, IsGoodPair t α := IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n : ℕ ↦ ⌊t * α ^ (n + 1)⌋). The statement itself can stay as {(t, α) | 0 < t ∧ 0 < α ∧ IsGoodPair t α} = answer(sorry).

findings.description:
The docstring presents this as "Erdős Problem 349, complete characterization on positive integer pairs" with answer (t,α) = (1,2). That answer is an artefact of IsGoodPair's conventions: indexing from n = 0 and counting values instead of terms.

In the source's sense (S(t,α) = (s₁,s₂,…), sums of distinct terms), the only complete positive integer pair is (1,1):
- S(1,1) = (1,1,1,…) is complete (machine-checked: IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n ↦ ⌊(1:ℝ)*1^(n+1)⌋));
- S(1,2) = (2,4,8,…) is not complete, since all sums are even (machine-checked);
- every other pair has all terms divisible by tα ≥ 2.
The same applies to one_two_isGoodPair ("(1,2) is good") and to dyadic_two_isGoodPair at k = 0.

The Lean statements are true of the current definition, but they are not results about the problem's notion, and they become false once IsGoodPair is made faithful.
findings.source_evidence: ErGr80 p. 57 and Graham 1964 §1: S(t,α) = (s₁, s₂, ...), sₙ = [tαⁿ]; completeness via P(S) = {Σ εₖsₖ : εₖ ∈ {0,1}} (ErGr80 §6, p. 53).
findings.suggested_fix: After fixing IsGoodPair, restate as `IsGoodPair t α ↔ t = 1 ∧ α = 1`, or reword the docstring so it does not claim to characterize Erdős 349 itself. Adjust one_two_isGoodPair and dyadic_two_isGoodPair (e.g. to (1/2, 2) and k ≥ 1) accordingly.

findings.description: True for the Lean definition. As a statement about the problem's notion (it is presented as "a partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349"), it fails at α = 1: S(t,1) = (⌊t⌋,⌊t⌋,…) is complete for 1 ≤ t < 2, since P(S) = ℕ (machine-checked for t = 1; IsGoodPair 1 1 is false). The docstring's argument ("every subset sum is bounded by the constant Σ_{i∈[0,⌊t⌋]} i") relies precisely on each value being counted once, which the source's P(S) does not do.
findings.source_evidence: ErGr80 §6, p. 53–54: P(A) = {Σ εₖaₖ : εₖ ∈ {0,1}, finitely many}; "the sums are restricted by the multiplicity any particular term can have". The book also treats sequences with repeated terms, e.g. "(F₁, ..., F₁, F₂, ..., F₂, ...)" (p. 55).
findings.suggested_fix: Under a faithful IsGoodPair, restrict to 0 < α < 1, and treat α = 1 separately: good iff 1 ≤ t < 2.

findings.description:
This is tagged research solved on the strength of Graham's theorem, which is about completeness of the sequence (terms counted with multiplicity). With the file's IsGoodPair the good α-sets are different, and so is their component structure. Heuristic computations (α-grid step 1/4000, sums up to 10^5, spot points checked exactly):
- t = 0.3: source components ≈ (1,1.755], [1.826,1.874], [1.882,1.957]; under IsGoodPair only the first and last remain. For example, α = 1.85 gives S = (1,1,3,6,12,…), which is complete, while its range is not.
- t = 0.7: IsGoodPair has an extra gap ≈ (1.624,1.690) inside Graham's Theorem 2 range. For example, α = 1.65 gives S = (1,1,3,5,8,…).
The Lean claim is plausibly still true: Graham's many components near α = 2 come from duplicate-free patterns (1,2,4,…), where the two notions agree. But it is not the cited result and would need its own argument.
findings.source_evidence: ErGr80 p. 57: "it is known [Gr (64) f] that for any k there exists t_k ∈ (0,1) so that {α : S(t_k,α) is complete} consists of more than k disjoint line segments". [Gr (64) f] = Graham, On a conjecture of Erdős in additive number theory, Acta Arith. 10 (1964), where completeness uses sums Σ εₖsₖ over indices.
findings.suggested_fix: This is resolved by fixing IsGoodPair (IsAddCompleteNatSeq' on n ↦ ⌊t·α^(n+1)⌋). The statement can then stay as is.

findings.description: The docstring asks "Is it true that the terms of the sequence ⌊(3/2)ⁿ⌋ are odd infinitely often and even infinitely often?", but the statement is only `answer(sorry) ↔ {n | Odd ⌊(3/2 : ℝ) ^ n⌋}.Infinite`. The even half is the sibling variant floor_3_halves_even.
findings.source_evidence: erdosproblems.com/349: "we do not even know whether ⌊(3/2)ⁿ⌋ is odd or even infinitely often"; ErGr80 p. 57: "we do not even know that [(3/2)ⁿ] is odd (or even) infinitely often".
findings.suggested_fix: Docstring: "Is it true that the terms of the sequence ⌊(3/2)ⁿ⌋ are odd infinitely often?"

reformulations.difference: The source's "{α : S(t_k,α) complete} consists of more than k disjoint line segments" is formalized as `k ≤ (connectedComponentIn S '' S).encard` with S = {α | 0 < α ∧ IsGoodPair t α}. That is, "at least k connected components" instead of "more than k segments", and the sequence is indexed from n = 0.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The claim is made for every k, so "> k for all k" ⟺ "≥ k for all k" (apply the latter at k+1). The segments are pairwise separated, so they are the connected components of their union. For t ∈ (0,1) the extra n = 0 term is ⌊t⌋ = 0, which changes no sums; Graham notes P(S_{t/α}(α)) = P(S_t(α)). Restricting to α > 0 loses nothing: for t < 1 and α ≤ 1 all terms are 0. This equivalence concerns the phrasing only. The separate IsGoodPair semantics issue is reported as a finding.

Erdos349.complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio: under the file's definition this is formally stronger than the source's conjecture (set-completeness implies sequence-completeness). The index shift is harmless under ∀ t > 0 (reparametrize t ↦ t/α). I did not prove that multiplicity is irrelevant for α < φ; numerical scans over α ∈ (1.02, φ), t ∈ (0,6) found no disagreement.
The 12 comments in the erdosproblems.com forum thread for #349 could not be read: Cloudflare blocks it and there is no archived snapshot.
The formal_proof links (a fork of formal-conjectures) were not consulted. I checked the truth of the auxiliary statements mathematically instead: all are true for the current definition.
review.notes:
Root cause: IsGoodPair uses `IsAddComplete (range ...)`, i.e. distinct values. The problem's sources (ErGr80 §6 and Graham 1964, on which the website's statement and remarks rely) define completeness of the sequence S(t,α) = (s₁, s₂, …) through P(S) = {Σ εₖsₖ}, so sums run over distinct indices.

Machine-checked (standard axioms only):
- /workspace/review/cex2.lean: `Cex.not_good : ¬ IsGoodPair (180/289) (17/10)`, via Folkman's argument.
- /workspace/review/cex3.lean: `Cex.source_complete : IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n : ℕ => ⌊(180/289 : ℝ) * (17/10) ^ (n+1)⌋)`, via Brown's criterion.
- /workspace/review/cex4.lean: `¬ IsGoodPair 1 1`; `IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n => ⌊(1:ℝ) * 1^(n+1)⌋)`; `¬ IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n => ⌊(1:ℝ) * 2^(n+1)⌋)`.

Numerics (/workspace/review/fscan.pl, chk.pl, comps.pl): the source-complete fraction of Graham's unit square reproduces his ≈ 0.85. Under IsGoodPair it is ≈ 0.81; all of the discrepancy lies in α ∈ (φ,2), where sequences start (1,1,3,…).

Precedent: PR #1217 (Erdős 354) replaced `IsAddComplete (range floors)` by `IsAddCompleteNatSeq'` for exactly this reason.

Declarations unaffected by the definitional issue:
- alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair and int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair stay true under a faithful definition.
- exists_finsetSum_two_pow is independent of it.

Other remarks:
- `answer(sorry)` at Prop elaborates to True by repository convention, so the (3/2)ⁿ variants read \"the set is infinite\". Both parity questions are open, as the source says.
- Graham 1964, Theorem 2, already proves the source's golden-ratio conjecture for 0 < t < 1, and even for α < 5^{1/3}. What remains open is t ≥ 1, so `research open` is correct for the conjecture as stated for all t > 0.
- No status issues found: erdosproblems.com (2026-08-24 snapshot) and the teorth database both record #349 as open.
- Metadata nits, not mathematics: exists_finsetSum_two_pow, one_two_isGoodPair and dyadic_two_isGoodPair are textbook-level but tagged `research solved`. Most formal_proof URLs point to a branch of a fork rather than a pinned commit.

demonstrated.claim: The file's definition disagrees with the source's completeness (sums of distinct terms of S(t,α) = (s₁, s₂, …), written with the repository's own `IsAddCompleteNatSeq'`) at concrete inputs: `¬ Erdos349.IsGoodPair 1 1` is proved although S(1,1) = (1,1,1,…) is complete, and (secondary point, indexing from n = 0) `Erdos349.IsGoodPair 1 2` is proved although S(1,2) = (2,4,8,…) is not complete.

Whatever set is filled in for `answer(sorry)`, the file's equation forces it to omit (1,1) and contain (1,2), while the source's answer set contains (1,1) and omits (1,2), so the requested set is not the source's answer set.

not_demonstrated.reason: Reported as questionable. Under the file's set-of-values definition its truth is not settled either way; it is plausibly true, but it is not the cited result. Any demonstration would need real mathematics (Graham's structure theorem), not a short computation.

Reported as questionable. It is true as stated about the file's definition, so there is nothing to prove or refute as formalized. The file's examples at (1,1) and (1,2) show why its answer (1,2) is not the source's: in the source's sense (1,1) is the only complete positive integer pair.
Reported as questionable. It is true as stated about the file's definition. Its divergence from the source's notion at α = 1 is exactly the (1,1) example shown for IsGoodPair.
Reported as a minor docstring mismatch only. The statement itself is a faithful open problem, so there is nothing to prove or refute.

submission.summary:
`/workspace/review/trivial_proof.lean` is 63 lines, compiles with no messages, and uses only standard axioms. It shows that `Erdos349.IsGoodPair` does not match the source's notion of a complete sequence.

- **Main defect (values vs. terms).** The file's definition takes subset sums of the *set* of values, whereas the source counts *terms* by index (the repository's `IsAddCompleteNatSeq'`). At (t, α) = (1, 1) the file proves `¬ IsGoodPair 1 1`, although S(1,1) = (1,1,1,…) is complete in the source's sense (that is also proved).
- **Secondary point (indexing from n = 0).** The file proves `IsGoodPair 1 2` via binary expansion, whereas the source's S(1,2) = (2,4,8,…) is not complete, since every sum of its terms is even.
- **Consequence for `Erdos349.erdos_349`.** Any set that makes the file's equation true must leave out (1,1) and include (1,2). The source's answer set does the opposite on both points.

The disagreement is not limited to the degenerate case α = 1. A non-degenerate witness is (t, α) = (180/289, 17/10), where S = (1,1,3,5,8,…): it is complete by Graham's Theorem 2, but `IsGoodPair` fails by Folkman's argument. I proved both halves in Lean earlier (`/workspace/review/cex2.lean`, `cex3.lean`, standard axioms only). That takes about 150 lines, so it is too long to count as trivial and is only mentioned in the file's header comment. Nothing under `/opt/formal-conjectures` was modified.

trivial_proof.lean:
import FormalConjectures.ErdosProblems.«349»

/-!
Erdős 349 (Erdős–Graham 1980, p. 57; Graham, Acta Arith. 10 (1964)) asks when the sequence
`S(t, α) = (s₁, s₂, …)`, `sₙ = ⌊t αⁿ⌋`, is *complete*, i.e. every large integer is `∑ εₖ sₖ`
with `εₖ ∈ {0, 1}`. Terms are counted by index, so a repeated value can be used as often as it
occurs. This is the repository's `IsAddCompleteNatSeq'` (sums over finite sets of indices).
`Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α` instead takes subset sums of the *set of values*
`Set.range (fun n ↦ ⌊t * α ^ n⌋)`, and it starts at `n = 0`.
The disagreement is not limited to `α = 1`. For example, with `t = 180/289` and `α = 17/10`,
`S = (1, 1, 3, 5, 8, 15, …)` is complete (Graham's Thm 2), but `IsGoodPair` fails by Folkman's
argument. That proof is longer and is not reproduced here.
-/

-- Erdos349.IsGoodPair: the file's definition says `(t, α) = (1, 1)` is NOT good, because the set
-- of values of `n ↦ ⌊1 * 1 ^ n⌋` is just `{1}`, so no integer `≥ 2` is a sum of distinct values.
theorem isGoodPair_one_one_false : ¬ Erdos349.IsGoodPair 1 1 := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := Filter.eventually_atTop.1 h
  obtain ⟨B, hB, hsum⟩ := hN (max N 2) (le_max_left _ _)
  have hB1 : B ⊆ {1} := fun x hx => by
    obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ := hB hx
    simp at hn
    simp [← hn]
  rcases Finset.subset_singleton_iff.1 hB1 with rfl | rfl <;> simp at hsum <;> omega

-- Erdos349.IsGoodPair: in the source's sense, however, `S(1, 1) = (1, 1, 1, …)` IS complete (`k`
-- is the sum of its first `k` terms), so the definition disagrees with the intended notion at `(1, 1)`.
example : IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n : ℕ ↦ ⌊(1 : ℝ) * 1 ^ (n + 1)⌋) :=
  Filter.eventually_atTop.2 ⟨0, fun k hk => ⟨Finset.range k.toNat, by simp; omega⟩⟩

-- Erdos349.IsGoodPair (secondary point, indexing from `n = 0`): the file's definition says `(1, 2)`
-- IS good, because its values `{1, 2, 4, …}` give every `k ≥ 0` by binary expansion.
theorem isGoodPair_one_two : Erdos349.IsGoodPair 1 2 := by
  refine Filter.eventually_atTop.2 ⟨0, fun k hk => ⟨k.toNat.bitIndices.toFinset.image ((2 : ℤ) ^ ·),
    fun x hx => ?_, ?_⟩⟩
  · obtain ⟨i, -, rfl⟩ := Finset.mem_image.1 hx
    exact ⟨i, show ⌊(1 : ℝ) * 2 ^ i⌋ = 2 ^ i by
      rw [one_mul, ← Int.cast_ofNat, ← Int.cast_pow, Int.floor_intCast]⟩
  · rw [Finset.sum_image fun i _ j _ h => pow_right_injective₀ (by norm_num) (by norm_num) h]
    have := Finset.sum_toFinset_bitIndices_two_pow k.toNat
    zify [hk] at this
    rw [this, Int.toNat_of_nonneg hk]

-- Erdos349.IsGoodPair (secondary point): the source's `S(1, 2) = (2, 4, 8, …)` (indexed from
-- `n = 1`) is NOT complete, because every sum of its terms is even.
example : ¬ IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n : ℕ ↦ ⌊(1 : ℝ) * 2 ^ (n + 1)⌋) := by
  intro h
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := Filter.eventually_atTop.1 h
  obtain ⟨B, hB⟩ := hN (2 * |N| + 1) (by cases abs_cases N <;> omega)
  have : Even (∑ i ∈ B, ⌊(1 : ℝ) * 2 ^ (i + 1)⌋) := Finset.even_sum _ fun i _ => by
    rw [one_mul, ← Int.cast_ofNat, ← Int.cast_pow, Int.floor_intCast, pow_succ]
    exact even_two.mul_left _
  rw [← hB] at this
  exact Int.not_even_two_mul_add_one _ this

-- Erdos349.erdos_349: whatever set is filled in for `answer(sorry)`, the file's equation forces it
-- to omit `(1, 1)` and to contain `(1, 2)`. The source's answer set does the opposite on both
-- points: `S(1, 1)` is complete and `S(1, 2)` is not (see above).
example (A : Set (ℝ × ℝ)) (h : {(t, α) | 0 < t ∧ 0 < α ∧ Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α} = A) :
    ((1 : ℝ), (1 : ℝ)) ∉ A ∧ ((1 : ℝ), (2 : ℝ)) ∈ A := by
  subst h
  exact ⟨fun h => isGoodPair_one_one_false h.2.2, ⟨one_pos, two_pos, isGoodPair_one_two⟩⟩

submission.summary:
I fixed the definition of `IsGoodPair` in `349.lean` and adjusted everything in the file that depended on it. The file compiles; the only warnings are the 12 `declaration uses sorry`, the same as before. Nothing else under the checkout was touched.

**The core fix.** `IsGoodPair t α` is now `IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n : ℕ ↦ ⌊t * α ^ (n + 1)⌋)`. This matches the source (ErGr80 §6, Graham 1964):
- The sequence is S(t,α) = (s₁, s₂, …) with sₙ = ⌊tαⁿ⌋, starting at n = 1.
- Sums run over distinct terms, so a value that appears at several indices can be used once per occurrence.

This is the index-based notion the repository already uses for Erdős 348 and 354.

**What this fixes.**
- `erdos_349` now asks for exactly the source's answer set. Its statement is unchanged; I only added a clarifying paragraph to its docstring.
- `exists_t_for_k_disjoint_segments` (unchanged text) now states Graham's theorem.
- `complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio` (unchanged text) now states exactly Erdős–Graham's conjecture.

**Checks against the new definition.** I compiled a copy of the edited file with test examples appended (in `/workspace/review/new_check.lean`). The pairs below are written (t, α).
- (180/289, 17/10) is good, as Graham's Theorem 2 says.
- (1, 1) is good.
- (1, 2) is not good.
- (1/2, 2) is good.

**Knock-on changes to the auxiliary results.** Several of these would have become false under the corrected definition, so I changed them minimally:
- `alpha_le_one_not_isGoodPair` was false at α = 1 for 1 ≤ t < 2. It is renamed `alpha_lt_one_not_isGoodPair` and now assumes α < 1; the docstring notes the α = 1 case.
- `one_two_isGoodPair` was false, because S(1,2) = (2,4,8,…) is not complete. It is renamed `one_half_two_isGoodPair` and now states `IsGoodPair (1 / 2) 2`.
- `dyadic_two_isGoodPair` gains the hypothesis `(hk : 0 < k)`.
- `integer_isGoodPair_iff`: the answer changes from (1,2) to (1,1).
- `alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair` and `int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair` are still true as written.

I also removed the `formal_proof` records from those six results. The linked proofs were written for the old definition and no longer prove these statements (PROOFS.md requires that they do). New proofs would have to be hosted outside this file. The record on `exists_finsetSum_two_pow` stays, since that lemma doesn't use `IsGoodPair`. Nothing else in the repository refers to the two renamed theorems; the only outside reference to this file, in `FC100SolvedSet1`, is to the unchanged `exists_t_for_k_disjoint_segments`.

**Smaller edits.** I fixed the minor docstring mismatch on `floor_3_halves_odd`, updated the other affected docstrings, and added ErGr80 and Gr64e (Graham, Acta Arith. 1964) to the module references.

module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-! # Erdős Problem 349

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980), p. 57.
- [Gr64e] Graham, R. L., On a conjecture of Erdős in additive number theory. Acta Arith. 10 (1964),
  63-70.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos349

open Set Filter Real Nat Function


/--
This defines the core property of the problem: the sequence $S(t,\alpha) = (s_1, s_2, \dots)$ with
$s_n = \lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is complete, i.e. every sufficiently large integer is a sum
$\sum_k \varepsilon_k s_k$ with $\varepsilon_k \in \{0, 1\}$, all but finitely many equal to $0$
[ErGr80, §6]. The sums are over distinct *terms*, not distinct values: a value that occurs at
several indices may be used once for each occurrence (for example, $S(1, 1) = (1, 1, 1, \dots)$
is complete).
-/
def IsGoodPair (t α : ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsAddCompleteNatSeq' (fun n : ℕ ↦ ⌊t * α ^ (n + 1)⌋)

/--
For what values of $t,\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ is the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ complete
(that is, all sufficiently large integers are the sum of distinct integers of the form $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$)?

As in [ErGr80] and [Gr64e], the sequence is $S(t,\alpha) = (s_1, s_2, \dots)$ with
$s_n = \lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$, and the sums are over distinct terms of $S(t,\alpha)$, so a value
occurring several times in the sequence may be used several times (see `IsGoodPair`).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_349 :
    {(t, α) | 0 < t ∧ 0 < α ∧ IsGoodPair t α} = answer(sorry) := by
  sorry

/--
It seems likely that the sequence is complete for all
for all $t>0$ and all $1 < \alpha < \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t)
    (hα : α ∈ Set.Ioo 1 ((1 + √5) / 2)) : IsGoodPair t α := by
  sorry

/--
For any $k$ there exists some $t_k\in (0,1)$ such that the set of $\alpha > 0$
such that the sequence $\lfloor t_k\alpha^n\rfloor$ is complete consists of at least $k$
disjoint line segments, that is, it has at least $k$ connected components.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem exists_t_for_k_disjoint_segments (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ t ∈ Ioo 0 1,
      let S := {α | 0 < α ∧ IsGoodPair t α}
      k ≤ (connectedComponentIn S '' S).encard := by
  sorry

/--
Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are odd infinitely often?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halves_odd :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {n | Odd ⌊(3/2 : ℝ) ^ n⌋}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Is it true that the terms of the sequence $\lfloor (3/2)^n\rfloor$ are even infinitely often?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_349.variants.floor_3_halves_even :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {n | Even ⌊(3/2 : ℝ) ^ n⌋}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- For $\alpha > 2$ and any $t > 0$, the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is not additively
complete; equivalently $(t, \alpha)$ is not a "good pair". A partial result on the open Erdős
Problem 349: it complements `complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio`. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t) (hα : 2 < α) : ¬ IsGoodPair t α := by
  sorry

/-- For $0 < \alpha < 1$ and any $t > 0$, $(t, \alpha)$ is not a good pair: $t\alpha^n \to 0$, so
all but finitely many terms $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ vanish, and only finitely many integers are
sums of distinct terms. (For $\alpha = 1$ the sequence is constant, equal to $\lfloor t\rfloor$,
and it is complete exactly when $1 \le t < 2$.) A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349,
complementing the $2 < \alpha$ and integer-coefficient cases. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem alpha_lt_one_not_isGoodPair (t α : ℝ) (ht : 0 < t) (hα0 : 0 < α) (hα1 : α < 1) :
    ¬ IsGoodPair t α := by
  sorry

/-- **Binary expansion.** Every natural number $k$ is a sum of distinct powers of two: there is
a finite set $E$ of exponents with $k = \sum_{i \in E} 2^i$. Proved by strong induction:
subtract the largest power $2^m \le k$, recurse on the remainder. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
  "https://github.com/cepadugato/formal-conjectures/blob/erdos-349-integer-characterization-proof/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/349.lean"]
theorem exists_finsetSum_two_pow (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ E : Finset ℕ, k = ∑ i ∈ E, 2 ^ i := by
  sorry

/-- **The pair $(1/2, 2)$ is good.** The terms $\lfloor \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 2^{n-1}$
($n \ge 1$) are the powers of two, which form a complete sequence: every $k \ge 1$ is a finite sum
of distinct powers of two. (By contrast, $S(1, 2) = (2, 4, 8, \dots)$ is not complete.) -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem one_half_two_isGoodPair : IsGoodPair (1 / 2) 2 := by
  sorry

/-- **The dyadic fiber at $\alpha = 2$.** For every $k \ge 1$, the pair $(1/2^k, 2)$ is good: the
term $\lfloor 2^n / 2^k\rfloor$ vanishes for $1 \le n < k$ and equals the exact power $2^{n-k}$ for
$n \ge k$, so the sequence consists of $k - 1$ zeros followed by all the powers of two, which form
a complete sequence. (For $k = 0$ the sequence $S(1, 2) = (2, 4, 8, \dots)$ is not complete.) -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem dyadic_two_isGoodPair (k : ℕ) (hk : 0 < k) : IsGoodPair (1 / 2 ^ k) 2 := by
  sorry

/-- **Integer leading coefficient $t \ge 2$ blocks completeness.** For every integer base
$\alpha$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ with integer $t \ge 2$ is not good: $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor =
t\alpha^n$ is a multiple of $t$, so every sum of distinct terms is too, but two consecutive large
integers cannot both be multiples of $t$. Generalizes the parity obstruction ($t = 2$). A partial
result on Erdős Problem 349. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair (t : ℤ) (ht : 2 ≤ t) (α : ℤ) :
    ¬ IsGoodPair (t : ℝ) (α : ℝ) := by
  sorry

/-- **Erdős Problem 349, complete characterization on positive integer pairs.** For integers
$t \ge 1$, $\alpha \ge 1$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ is good (i.e. $S(t, \alpha) = (t\alpha, t\alpha^2,
\dots)$ is complete) iff $(t, \alpha) = (1, 1)$: the sequence $S(1, 1) = (1, 1, 1, \dots)$ is
complete, while otherwise $t\alpha \ge 2$ divides every term $t\alpha^n$ ($n \ge 1$), hence every
sum of distinct terms. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem integer_isGoodPair_iff (t α : ℤ) (ht : 1 ≤ t) (hα : 1 ≤ α) :
    IsGoodPair (t : ℝ) (α : ℝ) ↔ t = 1 ∧ α = 1 := by
  sorry

end Erdos349
